annotations.text: FORMER RESIDENCE OF AN EARL-NOW A FARM TRAINING CENTRE.

Caldecott House near Cheshunt, once the residence of an Earl is now the centre of an educational experiment which gives a country boarding school training to 40 children of working-class parents who pay 10/- per week. The children whose ages range from two to 15 are taught farming and country life as well as scholastic subjects. Cows, Chickens, Rabbits and Coast are kept on the farmstead. The school will shortly celebrate the end of its first year on this estate. O.P.S. A girl and boy, pupils of the Barning School feeding the chickens with their daily corn.
THIUMAD OF HOLIDAYS.
The boys of the Plymouth Juvenile Trade School are partly sacrifice in all holidays in order to increase the output of emissions. Their chief work is the making of shell cases.

INSTEAD OF HOLIDAYS.
The boys of the Plymouth Juvenile Trade School are gladly sacrificing all holidays in order to increase the output of munitions. Their chief work is the making of shell cases.

WHILE FATHER IS FIGHTING, EIGHT-YEAR-OLD GIRL "RUNB" A SHOP, Alice Nestluke, who is only eight years of age, is managing a shop at 4, Anbren Vale, Hotwells, Bristol, while her father serves his Grandparent's country in the Navy. Her grandparents are looking after her for the present. Making up the accounts after the day's work.

SCHOOLBOYS AS BUILDERS.

One of the most interesting schools of London is the L.C.C. Training School for boys, situated between Brixton and Clapham. Here the boys are taught to be stone-masons, Carpenters, Joiners, Plumbers Decorators and architects. They wear smocks and overalls and work in model workshops. They draw their own plans and specifications, construct buildings, decorate walls and ceilings, make surveys, in fact do everything that builders,carpenters and masons do. The young builders are now at work on an auxiliary Restaurant and Refreshment room which they are building in their own hall. O.P.S. Boys in the Plumbing Department laying lead sheeting on a model flat roof. HD
BUILDING THEIR OWN CASTLE.
Ronald, son of Mr and Mrs Watson, makes ready to lay the bricks for their new home at Minster-on-See, after searching for four months for one. The new house, when built, is to be called Dunremyn.

BLUECOAT BOYS AS FARMERS.

A number of Christ's Hospital boys are shortly to leave for New Zealand to take up an agricultural career, and they are spending their vacation on an experimental farm at Horsham. With a view to developing Empire resources, the school keeps in touch with New Zealand.
Photo shows. Boys cutting a truss of hay.
BOX OF PIPETAN AS FORMAN

Mr. Ernest W. Hay, a led of fifteen at his work as foremen of the capping department of a Harleiden Electric Loop works. Run mainly by ex-officers "promotion according to merit" is the watchord of the concern, and in accordance with its spirit Ray will now have charge of from thirty to forty employees
BOLVING PETS' HOUSING PROBLEM。

The younger pupils of Maltman's Green School, Gérard's Cross are encouraged to become clever carpenters by making suitable homes for their pets. The children buy materials from the school shop with their pocket money and are encouraged to use them economically.
Photo shows...Pupils buying materials for their work at the school shop.
817 YEARS OLD FIRM.

Messrs R.W. Farman and Sons basket-makers, founded in IIo8 is still a flourishing concern at North Walsham. Norfolk, photo Shows.... Mr F Farman gives his son grandson Robert a lesson in basket-making.

FISHERBOYS' MUSEUM ON WHEELS.

Three fisherboys at Hastings have hit upon a novel plan for making pocket money. With a barrow stocked with starfish, sea urchins, squid, and other marine creatures, they lecture to holiday crowds on their specimens.

Photo shows... A youthful lecturer discourses on the characteristics of one of his many specimens.

William Albert Griffin, of Norbiton, who will be seven years old next month, is "quite beyond control."

His father, William Henry Griffin, said so on Saturday at Kingston-on-Thames Police Court, whether he was summoned for not sending William Albert to school regularly. The Bench talked of truant-schools.

But there is just one chance for this extremely youthful specimen of selfishness to escape official reformation. His sister Alice, who is thirteen, promised the magistrates that she would take him to school with her, and it was arranged that she should try to control the alleged uncontrollable.
So yesterday morning the twain set forth from their home at 1, Asylum-road, Norbiton, Alice clasping William Albert's reluctant hand firmly, and dutifully holding tightly to him, till the evening.

Their father, who is employed at a local tanyard, is, of course, unable to watch the boy continually himself, and claims that he has exhausted the ordinary methods of paternal coercion in vain. Chastissement with a twiggy stick he regards with disapproval, and rightly or wrongly thinks it would be useless.
CHILD-HOUSEKEEPER,
So everything now depends upon Alice, who has been housekeeper since the children's mother died quite recently.
Unless she can manage William Albert he must quit Asylum-road to become a boarder at a school where they are not so sparing of the use of twiggy sticks as is the head of his family.

Just before she died the mother told a school attendance officer, Mr. J. Williams, that, although she took him to school herself, the boy would run through another door into the street again after she had placed him in the porch.

Mr. Williams told the magistrates this, and added that often the boy, when his mother kept him in the house to take him to school, would break out cunningly and play truant for the day. Once when she had searched for him a long time she found him in the streets at midnight.
NOT A "RAEFLLES."
William Albert's father declared to the Bench that he could not do anything with his son.

The child is not an infant Raffles. He does not commit violent assaults upon strangers. He has never misappropriated a motor-car, or a canary, like a young desperate at Liverpool who was sent to a reformatory school not long ago.
It is simply that he loves not learning, and the "life adventurous" beckons to him perpetually, so that four walls cannot hold him last when the wandering humour has seized him.
It remains only to be seen whether Sister Alice can.
Perhaps some day, with the watchful care of his sister to guide him over these perplexing early years, he may develop into a great explorer.
But it is very hard work for Alice, though she struggles cheerfully and pluckily with her wayward little brother, and William Albert's resentful rebelliousness may vet turn to grateful docility.

Yesterday, however, she had to pulllustily to get him through the school door, both in the morning and in the afternoon. "And I have to keep both eyes wide open all the time," she said wistfully to The Daily Mirror.
